The Usual Suspects. A nineteen ninety-five crime thriller in which five career criminals are gathered for an apparent heist, only to discover they have been orchestrated by a legendary criminal kingpin.

Five career criminals are rounded up by police. Detective Kujan interrogates the sole survivor: Verbal Kint, a disabled con artist. As Kint narrates the story of their recent job, it becomes clear that an invisible force has orchestrated their downfall. A person named Keyser Soze, a notorious figure in the criminal underworld, has eliminated four of the five men.

Throughout the interrogation, Kujan and the audience assume Kint is a low-level participant. His physical infirmities and nervous demeanor make him seem harmless and inconsequential. Soze is mythologized through the testimonies as a legendary figure, a criminal so ruthless that his reputation alone inspires terror and obedience. He is a phantom within criminal networks, operating behind the scenes, shaping events while remaining invisible.

But then the final reveal arrives. Kint stands up. His limp disappears. His stutter evaporates. He walks away as a free man. He is Soze. The meek, seemingly broken interrogation subject is actually the terrifying mastermind. The film is narrated almost entirely by Kint's interrogation, making the audience complicit in both Kujan's and their own misreading of his character. Written by Christopher McQuarrie, who won the Academy Award for Original Screenplay, and directed by Bryan Singer, the film inverts the power dynamic of police questioning itself. The interrogation structure weaponizes audience perspective, forcing viewers to confront their own biases and assumptions about who deserves suspicion and who appears trustworthy.
